Charming Medieval Dinan, France: Why It’s a Must In Brittany (+ How to Spend Half a Day)

November 5, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 16:31
Instaread

As I planned my Brittany road trip with only a day or two to spend in this wild, beautiful place, I realllllly struggled to choose which places I could conceivably fit into my itinerary.  But one that rose to the top from the very beginning was Dinan.  And now post-trip, I 100% stand by that decision.

Dinan is the most well-preserved medieval town in Brittany, but more importantly it’s one that feels lived-in rather than a museum piece.  This isn’t a painstakingly recreated showpiece like Saint-Malo—it’s the real deal.  Boasting the oldest ramparts in Brittany, steep cobblestone streets, charming half-timbered buildings, quaint river harbor, and plenty of cozy cafes, Dinan is a perfect day trip from Saint-Malo and the coast, OR makes a perfect base for exploring the northern part of Brittany.

This post contains some affiliate links. I may earn a small commission from purchases made through clicks on these links (which I greatly appreciate, and at no extra cost to you). This helps support my independent trip planning content.  All opinions are, as always, completely my own.

My TL;dr on Dinan

If you’re road tripping Brittany, Dinan isn’t a maybe…it’s a must. It’s the best-preserved medieval town in the region and the perfect inland Brittany experience to pair with the coast.

If I only had one day in Brittany, I’d spend half of it here and the other half in Saint-Malo or out at Cap Fréhel. You only need about half a day to see the town, but I loved basing myself here. If you’re day-tripping in, I’d skip Sundays if possible, as a lot of the shops and restaurants aren’t open.

You might also like:  My Favorite Clean, Non-Toxic Sunscreen for Travel

Is Dinan worth it?

Yes, and unless you’ve already overdosed on medieval towns, it should be #1 or #2 on your itinerary list for northern Brittany (the Emerald Coast area).  With its half-timbered streets and river views from the ramparts, Dinan is the full authentic medieval experience that sits alongside Saint-Malo’s coastal fortress and views.

If you’re short on time, I’d definitely prioritize Dinan over Mont Saint-Michel, Dinard, Cancale (unless you’re the world’s biggest oyster fan), a full day in Saint-Malo (cut it to half-day), visiting Rennes, or going further south in Brittany.

How to get to Dinan

The best and most convenient way to visit Dinan—and indeed, Brittany—is with a rental car.  There is some public transportation in the area, but it’s limited and clunky to use.  Brittany is definitely best seen as a road trip, with beautiful country and coastal scenery dotted with tiny historic towns.

I took the TGV train from Paris-Montparnasse to Rennes, then picked up my rental car at the Rennes TGV station.  I usually use DiscoverCars, as super affordable, easy to use, and have a good rental company rating system, but I also always check Booking.com as well (who absorbed RentalCars.com).  My actual rental company this time was Europcar and I have no real complaints.

I parked at Parking Centre Historique, a small paid parking garage near my hotel (they gave me a parking pass so I didn’t have to pay).  This is very close to the Jardin Anglais and Basilique Saint-Sauveur, which is the starting place I recommend below.

Not up for driving in France, or only have one day and don’t want to hassle with a rental?  If you’re arriving in Rennes by train like I did, this private day trip with a local driver covers Dinan, Saint-Malo, and the oyster town of Cancale in one go. It’s a splurge, priced per group, so it makes the most sense if you’re splitting it with family or friends. Just know the driver isn’t a guide, so you’ll explore each town on your own.

Or arrive by boat up the Rance

If you’re staying in Saint-Malo or Dinard and want to make the trip itself part of the fun, you can actually sail into Dinan. Compagnie Corsaire runs a narrated cruise up the Rance River from Saint-Malo or Dinard, gliding past the tidal dam, little riverside villages, and locks before docking right at Dinan’s old port.

A few things to know before you book: the ride takes about 2 hours 45 minutes each way, it only runs in season (roughly April through early fall), and departure times shift with the tides. That means a round trip by boat leaves you very little time in town, so I’d do the boat one way and take the bus or a cab back. Compagnie Corsaire even sells a boat-plus-bus combo ticket on some dates.

Bonus: you’ll arrive at the bottom of the Rue du Jerzual, so you get the river port I missed.

If the boat schedule doesn’t work with your dates, this private day trip from Saint-Malo is the easiest car-free way to see Dinan, with stops at a few other nearby highlights too (including Mont Saint-Michel!). It’s another splurge-y per-group option, but you get door-to-door pickup and no tide timetables to worry about.

How much time do you need?

Dinan is quite small and it’s not full of things to *do”, per se, so it’s more about having the time to explore and soak in the vibes.  I’d say you should spend a day in Dinan max, but honestly half a day should be enough.

Timing is important though…because I was basing myself here, I ended up having an evening (late, Sunday, when everything was closed) and an early/mid morning (before much was open).  So that wasn’t as ideal for really getting to pop in and out of the shops or try restaurants on my list.  Ideally spend a half day here, from mid-morning through before dinner, or lunchtime through early evening (if you’re not basing yourself here).

How to spend a day (or less) in Dinan

Here is a rough plan for exploring Dinan, with a sample route.

  • I started at my B&B, Clos du Cedre.  The Jardin Anglais sits right outside, so take in that and the rampart views over the river first.
  • Circle the majestic Saint-Sauveur, then go inside.
  • Head into the half-timbered streets, including down the steep Rue du Jerzual and Rue du Petit Fort.
  • Down to the port, cross the old bridge, walk the river. (I missed this bit, and regret it)
  • Then climb back up (yeah, sorry, what goes down must come back up…)

Here’s a rough route for what I explored, though I also did a lot of backtracking up and down the narrow alleys and side streets.  Again, you really want to WANDER in DInan.  Further below I’ll talk about what you should definitely do beyond that end point—I didn’t have time, but you miss out on some cool stuff if you stop right there.

Let’s dive in…

You might also like:  My Favorite Non-Toxic Makeup Brand For Travel

Jardin Anglais and the ramparts

A few steps outside my adorable B&B was the trifecta of Jardin Anglais, the ramparts, and Basilique Saint-Sauveur.  I couldn’t really see what made the garden itself notable, but the other two are very cool.

There are around 2.7km of well-preserved medieval city walls encircling Dinan’s old town, including ten towers and four fortified gates.  From the ramparts you’ll get panoramic views over the Rance River valley, including the river port and some of the pretty half-timbered buildings.

Then turn around and head across the garden toward Basilique Saint-Sauveur.

You might also like:  The Google Flights ‘Map Search’ Hack You Should Be Using

Basilique Saint-Sauveur

This church is one of Dinan’s crown jewels, a majestic blend of Romanesque and Gothic styles jutting into the sky.  (Lol, a lot of sources call it Romanesque and “Flamboyant” Gothic, which is a new one for me and makes me laugh…)

It was commissioned in 1123, and added onto over the next few centuries.  It’s free to enter and definitely worth a few minutes of your time.

You might also like:  The BEIS Tote That’s Become My Go-To Airplane “Personal Item”

There are medieval “recumbent” tombs like this gentleman…I love how his pointy soft slippered toes curl over his…cat?? (Update: turns out it’s a lion, which I guess is more on-brand for a knight…)

The stained glass windows were replaced more recently but I am convinced that the top-left person (third photo below) is Frankenstein’s monster, and that the top-right is Voldemort, and no one can tell me otherwise…

You might also like:  10 Places I’m Dying to Visit in 2027

Medieval half-timbered houses, including Rue du Jerzual & Rue du Petit Fort

The biggest draw in Dinan is its very well-preserved—and super cute—medieval half-timbered houses.  The best thing you can do is wander around down different streets and alleys, but here are some you should try to hit.

  • Grande Rue → Place des Cordeliers → Place des Merciers. This is your half-timbered core.
  • Rue de l’Apport. It has the overhanging upper floors and jutting windows that give Dinan that quintessential look.
  • Rue de l’Horloge. Walk past the clock tower and the Maison du Gisant, one of the town’s most famous houses.
  • Rue de la Cordonnerie and Rue du Petit-Pain have more corbelled houses if you want a bonus loop.
  • Rue de la Lainerie → Rue du Jerzual → Rue du Petit Fort. A must-see.  The cobbled street dates to at least the 12th century, lined with half-timbered houses.  It drops steeply all the way down to the old bridge, becoming Rue du Petit Fort near the water. Look out for the Maison du Gouverneur, which is half-timbered on three sides.

From the church I headed downhill on Rue de l’Apport to Place des Merciers, but it is worth the little jog over to Rue de l’Horloge.  Honestly I wasn’t looking closely at the streets, because there was so much to see—I just tried to stick to the streets and alleys that were packed with the half-timbered houses.

You definitely have to walk down the Rue du Jerzual and through the Porte du Jerzual—a cool fortified gate/tower dating to the 14th century.  From here the street changes to the Rue du Petit-Fort and onward to its conclusion at the medieval bridge over the River Rance.

I walked down past the Porte du Jerzual, realized I wasn’t sure what was actually waiting at the bottom, and turned back to save time. Don’t be me!

The street continues as the Rue du Petit Fort down to the old stone bridge, the riverside quays with cute café terraces, and the view up to the viaduct.  Budget an extra 45–60 minutes for the full walk down and back up.

What I missed

As I just mentioned, I was running short on time and needed to head toward the Loire Valley, so I ended up skipping the river port and old bridge.  Make sure to budget time for that—cross the old bridge, walk the river, and have lunch or a drink on the quay.  Haha, fortify yourself for the climb back up because it is a doozy.

I somehow missed the Donjon de la Duchesse Anne and Eglise Saint-Malo de Dinan, the other cool church in town (but if you have to pick one, definitely go for Basilica Saint-Sauveur!).

Where to eat

I ended up at Brasserie Zaizai two nights in a row due to slim pickin’s on Sunday and Monday nights.  I had a couple great cocktails.  My food was all good, and the smash burger and fries were great.  It’s in the old train station, outside the old town (but very easily walkable).  Its Sunday brunch (11–3, by reservation) can be a great option if you visit on Sunday and other places are closed.

There was a kouign amann shop called Steeve McKouign that gets great reviews and wasn’t open and I’M STILL MAD ABOUT IT.  That is the best name.  The kouign amann I did end up eating (from a bakery whose name I have apparently blocked out) was a total letdown, and I didn’t even finish it. If you know me, you know that’s a tragedy. Steeve, I’m coming back for you.

Where to stay in Dinan

I stayed at the lovely Clos du Cedre B&B in Dinan, but it was a super tough choice…this lovely boutique hotel and this character-filled hotel in a half-timbered building were also on my short list and both looked amazing.

Clos du Cedre was right next to the Basilique Saint-Sauveur church and just steps from a great view from the ramparts over the river Rance.  The owner was very welcoming and the house is beautiful and cozy.  My room was spacious and there’s a nice little breakfast served with homemade jams in the morning.  I’d absolutely stay here again!

Weather and packing tips

I was visiting Brittany in mid-May, and was surprised that the weather was not as warm as I’d assumed—I thought it would feel like real summer.  But the forecast overall was highs around upper 50s/low 60s F and lows of around 50 F.  While it can get hot here sometimes, you’d be wise to expect some clouds, rain showers, and wind, so it can still feel a bit chilly sometimes.  Layers are your friend!

For the Brittany portion of my trip and in Dinan, I relied on my favorite lightweight stretchy travel pants (Athleta Brooklyn and these Eddie Bauer ones are my faves), and some jeans.  I paired the pants with lightweight tops and a light cardigan.

Shoes-wise, in Brittany I wore my cute white sneakers and my Rothy’s flats and had my cute raincoat and lightweight scarf for cool mornings and a rainy evening.  These non-tox beauty products always travel with me, and I did my entire 9-day trip in my favorite carry-on suitcase and my giant tote “personal item”.

FAQs

Is Dinan worth visiting?

Absolutely. Dinan is the most authentic medieval town in Brittany, with half-timbered streets and ramparts that feel lived-in rather than staged. If you’re road tripping northern Brittany, I’d put it at the top of your list alongside Saint-Malo.

How much time do you need in Dinan?

Half a day is enough to see the highlights without feeling rushed.  A full day, max.  Mid-morning through late afternoon is the sweet spot, when shops and cafés are open.

Can you visit Dinan and Saint-Malo in the same day?

Yes. They’re only about half an hour apart by car, so a half day in each works well. If I only had one day in Brittany, that’s exactly how I’d spend it.

Can you get to Dinan without a car?

You can, but it’s not the easiest. The most scenic option is the boat up the Rance River from Saint-Malo (seasonal, roughly April through early November, with times set by the tides), but the trip takes a few hours each way, so most people take the bus back. Regional buses exist but are limited, which is why I’d rent a car for Brittany.  If you’d rather skip public transit entirely, a private day trip from Saint-Malo or Rennes is the easiest option (I’ve linked a couple above).

Is Dinan open on Sundays?

Yes, you can absolutely visit the town.  But here, as in a lot of small French towns, many shops and restaurants close on Sundays, and dinner options can be thin on Sunday and Monday nights, at least in shoulder season. If you’re day-tripping, I’d pick another day if that’s possible—if not, it’s still worth visiting. If you’re staying over, plan or book those dinners ahead.

Where should you park in Dinan?

Park outside or at the edge of the old town and walk in, since the medieval streets are narrow and steep. I used the small paid Parking Centre Historique near the Jardin Anglais and Basilique Saint-Sauveur, which is also the perfect starting point for exploring.

Is Dinan a good base for exploring Brittany?

Yes, and I loved staying here. Saint-Malo, Cap Fréhel and Fort La Latte are all easy day trips, and you get Dinan’s quiet evenings and mornings to yourself after the day-trippers leave.
